import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import SymLogNorm

RTCB_GO_LIVE = pd.Timestamp("2025-12-05")  # RTC+B went live Dec 5, 2025
TZ = "America/Chicago"


def plot_rtcb(prices, location=None):
    df = prices.copy()
    ts = pd.to_datetime(df["interval_start_local"], utc=True, errors="coerce")
    df["ts"] = ts.dt.tz_convert(TZ).dt.tz_localize(None)
    df = df.dropna(subset=["ts", "spp"])

    loc = location or df["location"].value_counts().idxmax()
    d = df[df["location"] == loc].copy()
    d["date"] = d["ts"].dt.normalize()
    d["hour"] = d["ts"].dt.hour
    d["era"] = np.where(d["date"] >= RTCB_GO_LIVE, "After RTC+B", "Before RTC+B")
    colors = {"Before RTC+B": "#7aa2ff", "After RTC+B": "#ff5c8a"}
    heat = d.pivot_table(index="hour", columns="date", values="spp", aggfunc="mean")

    with plt.style.context("dark_background"):
        fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
            2, 1, figsize=(14, 9), facecolor="#0b0f19",
            gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.3, 1]},
        )
        for ax in (ax1, ax2):
            ax.set_facecolor("#0b0f19")
            ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

        # Top: date x hour heatmap
        x = heat.columns.values
        vmax = max(300, np.nanpercentile(heat.values, 99))
        im = ax1.pcolormesh(
            x, np.arange(24), heat.reindex(range(24)).values, cmap="magma",
            shading="nearest", norm=SymLogNorm(linthresh=30, vmin=-50, vmax=vmax),
        )
        ax1.set_ylim(23.5, -0.5)
        ax1.set_yticks(range(0, 24, 3))
        ax1.set_yticklabels([f"{h:02d}:00" for h in range(0, 24, 3)])
        ax1.set_ylabel("Hour of day (CT)")
        ax1.set_title(f"ERCOT real-time SPP at {loc}  |  hour of day x date",
                      loc="left", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold")
        if x.min() <= RTCB_GO_LIVE <= x.max():
            ax1.axvline(RTCB_GO_LIVE, color="#00f0c8", lw=2, ls="--")
            ax1.text(RTCB_GO_LIVE, 22.8, "  RTC+B go-live", color="#00f0c8",
                     fontsize=11, va="center", ha="left", fontweight="bold",
                     bbox=dict(facecolor="#0b0f19", alpha=0.75, edgecolor="none", pad=2))
        fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax1, pad=0.01, fraction=0.025).set_label("$/MWh (symlog)")

        # Bottom: typical daily shape, before vs after
        for era, g in d.groupby("era"):
            prof = g.groupby("hour")["spp"].quantile([0.1, 0.5, 0.9]).unstack()
            ax2.fill_between(prof.index, prof[0.1], prof[0.9], color=colors[era], alpha=0.18)
            ax2.plot(prof.index, prof[0.5], color=colors[era], lw=3,
                     label=f"{era} (median, p10-p90)")
        ax2.set_xlim(0, 23)
        ax2.set_xticks(range(0, 24, 2))
        ax2.set_xlabel("Hour of day (CT)")
        ax2.set_ylabel("$/MWh")
        ax2.set_title("Typical daily price shape, before vs after", loc="left", fontsize=13)
        ax2.grid(alpha=0.15)
        ax2.legend(frameon=False)

        fig.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
    return fig


fig = plot_rtcb(prices)                 # busiest location
# fig = plot_rtcb(prices, "HB_HOUSTON")  # or pick one

title: ERCOT Analysis
text:
ERCOT, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, operates the power grid for most of Texas and runs its wholesale electricity market. The grid is divided into four load zones: Houston, North, South, and West. On December 5, 2025, ERCOT launched Real-Time Co-optimization plus Batteries (RTC+B), a redesign of its real-time market. Under RTC+B, energy and ancillary services are dispatched together every five minutes, and batteries are modeled as single units. ERCOT’s goal was to give the grid more flexibility in real time and to procure energy and ancillary services more efficiently. This analysis examines how price spreads between the four load zones differ before and after RTC+B went live. Because the post-RTC+B period is short and covers different seasonal conditions, these comparisons show associations, not proof that RTC+B caused the changes.
The first graph shows the number of extreme price spreads by month. An extreme price spread is defined as a price spread between load zones that is in the 95th percentile of Pre-RTC+B price spreads. The graph shows that Post-RTC+B tends to have less extreme price spreads.









This next graph shows the median price spread by the hour of the day. The median spread Pre-RTC+B is higher than Post-RTC+B before 12:00 but lower after. This could show the RTC+B’s effect on efficiently storing energy throughout the day.









These next three graphs show the Western load zone’s median price difference compared to the other three load zones in ERCOT. One trend that emerges from the plots is that Post-RTC+B tends to have lower price difference between load zones with the exception of the Houston load zone, which is more volatile.

title: ERCOT Ancillary Analysis
text:
Ancillary services are services that support the reliable operation of the electricity grid by maintaining the balance between supply and demand, for example by providing reserve energy during outages or congestion. MCPC is the Market Clearing Price for Capacity, the price paid for each ancillary service in a given interval.
In this analysis of ERCOT’s ancillary services, we found a large initial spike in the daily median price after the launch of RTC+B, which then settled to a level slightly above the pre-RTC+B baseline for the same time of year in 2024.
